notes.summary: Why study languages when you already know a few? Because every language is a bundle of design decisions — evaluation order, typing discipline, memory model — and understanding the design space makes you a better programmer in ANY language. CSE341 (Dan Grossman's celebrated UW course) studies programming languages by building interpreters, using the PLAI book as its spine.
notes.focus: Install Racket (plt.org) and DrRacket today — the entire course happens inside it. Then read PLAI chapter 1 and note the three dimensions Grossman says matter most.

notes.summary: Racket's prefix syntax is s-expressions — trees written as text. You learn the core forms (define, cond, let, lambda), evaluation as substitution, and the REPL workflow. The parens stop being noise once you see them as the AST printed directly: no operator precedence, ever.
notes.focus: Rewrite three Python functions in Racket. The friction you feel IS the course's first lesson — different designs expose different ideas.

notes.summary: First-class functions, deeply: lexical scope, closures capturing environments, and the classic higher-order combinators (map/filter/fold as USER-defined, not built-ins). This extends CS61A's treatment with a key new lens: you will soon implement closures yourself in your own interpreter.
notes.focus: Define map, filter, and fold from scratch in Racket, then compose them to process a nested list. When abstractions become user-defined, you own them.

notes.summary: Variant datatypes (one of several shapes) with pattern matching: define once, destruct everywhere, with the compiler checking exhaustiveness. This is the ML/Rust/enum pattern that eliminates whole classes of null/flag bugs. Racket structs and match give you the full experience.
notes.focus: Define an arithmetic-expression datatype (num/add/mul) and write eval with match. You've just built the AST your compiler in N2T used — now in 10 lines.

notes.summary: Tail calls: when the recursive result needs no further work, the language reuses the stack frame — iteration and recursion unify. Accumulator-passing style turns naive tree-recursive functions into tail-recursive ones. Functional languages run loops as recursion by design, and now you know the mechanism.
notes.focus: Rewrite length and reverse with accumulators, then explain why the naive reverse is O(n^2). The accumulator insight generalizes to every traversal.

notes.summary: Hindley-Milner type inference: write no annotations, get full static types — unification over constraints does the work. Polymorphic types ('a -> 'a) fall out for free. You learn what your 6.100L-era Java generics actually mean, and why ML's type system catches nulls at compile time.
concepts: Types as theorems, programs as proofs
notes.focus: Hand-infer the type of a compose function by writing constraints and unifying. Ten minutes of inference by hand makes compilers' error messages legible.

notes.summary: Adding state to a functional core: boxes/cells, aliasing (your 6.100L term-1 lesson returning), equality vs identity, and the reasoning cost mutation imposes. The lecture frames purity as a DESIGN choice with real benefits (equational reasoning, parallelism) — the argument that produced Rust's ownership later.
notes.focus: Write a counter with a closure over a box, then draw the aliasing when two counters share a cell. State diagrams never go out of style.

notes.summary: Call-by-value vs call-by-name vs call-by-need: when do arguments evaluate? Lazy evaluation makes infinite streams first-class (cons with thunks), memoizing as it goes. Haskell's purity exists largely to make laziness safe — evaluation order as a visible design decision, not an implementation detail.
notes.focus: Define an infinite stream of naturals in lazy Racket and take the first 10. Infinite data that works is the moment laziness clicks permanently.

notes.summary: The course's centerpiece: implement an interpreter for a small functional language. Substitution model first (clean but slow), then environments (closures capture them). You wrote a Scheme interpreter's cousin in CS61A — this one goes deeper, with each design decision (shadowing, recursion) an explicit choice.
notes.focus: Implement your interpreter's environment lookup, then add let shadowing. Watching scope rules appear as LINES OF CODE demystifies every language you know.

notes.summary: The grand comparison: dynamic typing's flexibility vs static typing's guarantees; OOP's subtype hierarchies vs functional pattern matching; Ruby-style classes vs closures. No winner is declared — the point is the ability to argue both sides with evidence, choosing per project.
notes.focus: Write the same data-processing program twice — once OO with inheritance, once functional with match — and list where each hurt. Your own pain data beats any textbook claim.

notes.summary: Structuring programs beyond functions: modules as namespaces with sealed implementations, abstract data types enforced by signatures (ML's opaque ascription), and contracts as runtime-checked interfaces between components. The design lesson generalizes across every language you know — from Java packages to TypeScript modules to API boundaries.
notes.focus: Take one datatype you've built and hide its representation behind a module signature. Then try to break the abstraction from outside — failing to is the exercise.

notes.summary: Checkpoint across the functional core: evaluation, closures, datatypes, inference, laziness, and your interpreter's environment model. The exam style here is 'what does this program evaluate to, and WHY' — semantic reasoning, written precisely. Your CS61A and interpreter work are the direct prerequisites.
notes.focus: For five tricky programs, predict the result BEFORE running. The gap between prediction and reality is precisely your midterm study list.

notes.summary: The finale: macros as programs writing programs (Racket's superpower), and the course synthesis — every paradigm you studied is a point in the design space, and YOU can now build a language choosing any of them. Your CS143 compilers course next term is the natural continuation: interpreters there, translation here.
notes.focus: Write one macro (unless) and reflect: you just extended the language itself. Then draw the course map — evaluation, types, state, paradigms — as your final artifact.
